This robustness is validated by rigidly rearranging latent codes via 2D rotation; models with local coordinate systems maintain lower FID scores under rearrangement compared to global coordinate systems [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the authors trained GSN with both global and local coordinate systems to validate the hypothesis of feature sharing. They performed a 'rigid re-arrangement of latent codes in W by applying a 2D rotation' and measured FID. The text concludes that 'A local coordinate system is significantly more robust to rearranging local latent codes than a global one,' which aligns with the claim that models with local coordinate systems maintain lower FID scores (implied by higher robustness/better performance) under rearrangement compared to global coordinate systems.

GSN decomposes a scene into many independent locally conditioned radiance fields to improve generative performance over global conditioning methods like GRAF [S1].

It further provides quantitative results (Table 3) showing that GSN with local latents outperforms GSN with global latents, and the notes confirm that GRAF uses global conditioning while GSN uses locally conditioned radiance fields.

The method was developed to address limitations in global conditioning approaches for generative modeling of radiance fields [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that GSN uses 'locally conditioned radiance fields' and compares this approach to GRAF and π-GAN which use 'global conditioning'. Furthermore, the text demonstrates that decomposing the scene into independent locally conditioned radiance fields improves performance (lower FID scores) over using a global latent code. This supports the claim that the method was developed to address limitations (specifically performance issues) associated with global conditioning approaches.

This decomposition allows the scene to be modeled as many independent locally conditioned radiance fields, which drastically improves generative performance (e.g., reducing FID from 68.42 to 41.75 and SwAV-FID from 6.14 to 4.14 in ablation studies) [S1].

The claim states that decomposing the scene into independent locally conditioned radiance fields improves generative performance, specifically citing FID reduction from 68.42 to 41.75 and SwAV-FID from 6.14 to 4.14. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Table 3, showing that 'GSN + global latents' (representing the non-decomposed/global conditioning baseline) has an FID of 68.42 and SwAV-FID of 6.14, while 'GSN + local latents' (representing the decomposition into locally conditioned fields) has an FID of 41.75 and SwAV-FID of 4.14. The text also states that 'Generative performance can be improved by decomposing the scene into many independent locally conditioned radiance fields'. Thus, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.
supported
Instead of a single global latent vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^c$ that conditions the entire radiance field $f_\theta$, GSN uses a local latent grid $W \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}$ [S1].

The claim states that GSN uses a local latent grid $W$ instead of a single global latent vector $w$. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the notes ('GSN uses a local latent code representation $W$... compared to a global latent code $w$') and in the passages ('We compare the effect of replacing our local latent codes W... with a global latent code w...'). The mathematical dimensions provided in the claim ($W$ as a grid, $w$ as a vector) are consistent with the textual description of a 'local latent grid' versus a 'global latent code'.
